title: BUG: StandardScaler.partial_fit replaces an existing variance with NaN when a new dense batch has an all-NaN feature
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm exploring numerical reliability in scientific Python through AI-assisted investigation and testing.
This issue came from checking how StandardScaler.partial_fit handles batches with missing observations and comparing incremental results with batch fitting.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

After StandardScaler learns valid statistics for a feature, a subsequent dense batch containing only NaNs in that feature changes its var_ and scale_ to NaN, while its mean_ and sample count remain correct.

In the recorded checks, this also causes finite values in that feature to be transformed to NaN.

The StandardScaler documentation states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting. The example below supplies no new valid observations for the first feature.

Documentation:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html

Related work:
PR #16466 included preserving sparse incremental statistics when a new batch contributes zero valid observations, including all-NaN second-batch tests. This report concerns the dense-array counterpart.
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/16466

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

A = np.array([[1., 10.], [3., 20.]])
B = np.array([[np.nan, 30.], [np.nan, 40.]])

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.partial_fit(A)
np.testing.assert_allclose(scaler.var_, [1., 25.])

scaler.partial_fit(B)
np.testing.assert_allclose(scaler.var_[0], 1.)
```

### Expected Results

The final assertion should pass. After processing B, the first feature should retain its mean of 2, variance of 1, scale of 1, and sample count of 2, because B contains no new non-missing observations for that feature.

The second feature should have a mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4.

### Actual Results

The final assertion fails because the variance of the first feature becomes NaN.

After processing B, the first feature has a mean of 2, variance of NaN, scale of NaN, and sample count of 2. The mean and sample count remain correct, but the previously valid variance and scale are lost.

The second feature has the expected mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4.

The update also emits RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in divide.

### Versions

```shell
Reproduced with scikit-learn 1.8.0 and 1.9.1, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0, and Python 3.12.14 on Linux x86_64.

Summary of sklearn.show_versions() from the scikit-learn 1.9.1 reproduction environment (filesystem paths omitted):

System:
- Python: 3.12.14 (main, Aug 25 2026, 14:00:49) [Clang 22.1.3]
- Machine: Linux-6.18.44-x86_64-with-glibc2.41

Python dependencies:
- scikit-learn: 1.9.1
- pip: 25.0.1
- setuptools: 84.0.0
- NumPy: 2.3.5
- SciPy: 1.17.0
- Cython: None
- pandas: 2.2.3
- matplotlib: 3.10.8
- joblib: 1.5.3
- threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
- narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True

Threadpool information:
- NumPy and SciPy BLAS: OpenBLAS 0.3.30, pthreads, SkylakeX
- OpenMP runtime: libgomp
- sklearn.show_versions() reported 5 threads for each runtime; the numerical validation runs used a one-thread limit.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a fix after maintainer triage, with AI assistance.

My investigation points to the dense incremental variance update when a feature receives zero new non-missing observations. A possible strategy is to preserve the existing statistics for that feature when it already has valid observations, while updating the other features normally.

I have tested a limited local prototype for this case. It is not yet a general fix and does not address features that have no valid observations in the initial batch. I would start with a regression test for the example above and discuss the intended scope with the maintainers before opening a PR.

title: ENH Ridge: support `solver="cholesky"` for array API inputs
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Credit to @ogrisel for the idea.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

With array API dispatch, `Ridge` only supports `solver="svd"`, and `solver="auto"` resolves to `"svd"` with a warning (#27800 started with SVD only). The SVD is much more expensive than the Cholesky path used for NumPy inputs, so `Ridge` on GPU is often slower than `Ridge` on CPU with NumPy, and sometimes much slower.

I'd like `solver="cholesky"` (and so `solver="auto"`) to work with array API inputs, and be fast on GPU.

### Describe your proposed solution

Split the Cholesky solver in two: compute the Gram matrix on the device (`X.T @ X`, or `X @ X.T` in the dual case when `n_features > n_samples`), move it to the host, and solve it with the existing NumPy/SciPy code. Then move the coefficients back to the device:

```python
def _solve_cholesky_array_api(X, y, alpha, xp):
    n_samples, n_features = X.shape
    dual = n_features > n_samples
    G = X @ X.T if dual else X.T @ X  # the expensive part, on the device
    rhs = y if dual else X.T @ y
    G, rhs = _convert_to_numpy(G, xp), _convert_to_numpy(rhs, xp)
    # same solve as for NumPy inputs: scipy.linalg.solve(..., assume_a="pos")
    if dual:
        coef = _solve_cholesky_kernel(G, rhs, alpha)
    else:
        coef = _solve_cholesky_gram(G, rhs, alpha)  # _solve_cholesky, minus the Gram matrix
    coef = xp.asarray(coef, device=device(X))
    if dual:
        coef = X.T @ coef
    return coef
```

Let's call this policy A. The system to solve is only `(n_features, n_features)` (or `(n_samples, n_samples)`), so the host solve and the transfers are cheap compared to the Gram matrix. And the solve behaves exactly like for NumPy inputs, whatever the namespace: same SPD solver, same `LinAlgError` handling for singular systems.

`solver="auto"` could then resolve to `"cholesky"` for array API inputs, like for NumPy inputs, and the warning would go away.

I prototyped it by swapping `_solve_svd` during `Ridge.fit` (`fit_intercept=True`, `alpha=1.0`, one target, standard normal data, best of 3 after a warmup, torch 2.13). Coefficients match the NumPy Cholesky solver to ~1e-6 in float32 and ~1e-14 in float64. Fit times in seconds, policy B is the fully on-device alternative described below:

NVIDIA L4, NumPy on 8 vCPUs (AMD EPYC 7R13):

| shape | dtype | NumPy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy A | policy B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.13 | 0.091 | 0.011 | 0.011 |
| 500,000 x 100 | float64 | 0.20 | 0.45 | 0.059 | 0.059 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.27 | 0.21 | 0.024 | 0.018 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.44 | 2.3 | 0.29 | 0.28 |
| 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.9 | not run | 0.15 | 0.15 |
| 463,810 x 990 | float64 | 3.6 | not run | 2.5 | 2.5 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.52 | 1.5 | 0.12 | 0.044 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.93 | 13 | 0.80 | 0.69 |
| 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 3.1 | not run | 0.66 | 0.27 |

Intel Arc B390 iGPU (Panther Lake), NumPy on the 16 cores of the Core Ultra X7 358H:

| shape | dtype | NumPy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy A | policy B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.12 | 0.49 | 0.021 | 0.021 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.14 | 1.1 | 0.037 | 0.036 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.35 | 2.0 | 0.27 | 0.27 |
| 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.1 | not run | 0.30 | 0.30 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.27 | 10 | 0.11 | 0.075 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.66 | 17 | 0.79 | 0.71 |
| 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 2.5 | not run | 0.85 | 0.74 |

Policy A is 7x to 90x faster than the current SVD, and in float32 2.5x to 13x faster than NumPy on CPU. In float64, with ~1000 features or more, it is only 0.8x to 1.5x the speed of NumPy: both GPUs have a low float64 throughput (~450 GFLOP/s measured on the Arc B390), and the Gram matrix is a float64 matmul.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Policy B: solve on the device with `xp.linalg.solve`, which is in the array API `linalg` extension.

It is faster than policy A only when the system to solve is large, in practice in the dual case: up to 2.7x in float32 on the L4. Elsewhere both are within noise, because the Gram matrix dominates.

But each namespace handles the solve its own way, and checking them all is hard. For instance, on a singular system `torch.linalg.solve` raises a `_LinAlgError`, while `cupy.linalg.solve` returns NaNs by default. Some namespaces may also not implement the `linalg` extension. Policy A avoids all of this by reusing the code path we already test with NumPy.

### Additional context

#34793 (centering trick for the Cholesky solver) would help here too: it avoids the centered copy of `X`, which halves the device memory needed by `fit`.

I'd go with policy A. We could switch the solve to the device later for large systems if it turns out to matter.

title: FeatureAgglomeration.inverse_transform fails on list/DataFrame input, including its own set_output result
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I work in AI, ML, DS and use scikit-learn for preprocessing and modeling pipelines, usually with set_output(transform="pandas").

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`FeatureAgglomeration.inverse_transform` indexes its input directly (`X[..., inverse]`) without validating it, so anything that isn't a numpy array fails, including the pandas/polars output that `set_output` makes the estimator itself return.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import FeatureAgglomeration

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 4)
fa = FeatureAgglomeration(n_clusters=2).fit(X)

fa.inverse_transform([[1.0, 2.0]])      # TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple

fa.set_output(transform="pandas")
fa.inverse_transform(fa.transform(X))   # pandas InvalidIndexError
```

### Expected Results

Same result as passing the equivalent ndarray (the docstring says X is array-like of shape (n_samples, n_clusters) or (n_clusters,)).

### Actual Results

- list: `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple`
- pandas (including the estimator's own `set_output(transform="pandas")` output): `InvalidIndexError` / `KeyError`
- polars: `DuplicateError`

A plain ndarray works.

### Versions

```shell
scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6, polars 1.44.2, numpy 2.5.3 (main has the same code).
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes. I have a fix (validate with `check_array(X, ensure_2d=False)` in `inverse_transform`, plus tests for list/pandas/polars/1-D input) and would like to open the PR once this is triaged.

Found with AI assistance (Claude); I verified the repro.

title: ARDRegression.scores_ combines updated precisions with the previous posterior
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Luis. I’m starting to contribute to scikit-learn by working through focused issues in its Bayesian linear models. I noticed this behavior while investigating `ARDRegression` after the discussion on #35026, and wanted to report a reproducible example before proposing a change.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `compute_score=True`, `ARDRegression` computes the posterior covariance and coefficients, updates `alpha_` and `lambda_`, then calculates `scores_` using the **updated precisions** but the **previous covariance and residual sum of squares**. As a result, the last score can differ from the objective evaluated at the fitted parameters. This can mislead users who inspect `scores_` to monitor optimization or compare the final score with an evaluation at the fitted parameters. Fitted coefficients and predictions appear unaffected

This is separate from whether the objective should include normalization constants: the comparison below omits the same constants as the current implementation.

If `scores_[-1]` is intended to report the objective at the fitted parameters, its covariance, coefficients, residuals, and precisions should correspond to the same parameter state.

There is also a related question for pruning: once the active feature set is stable, the determinant uses the covariance of retained features, while the score sums `log(lambda_)` over **all** features. Should the score represent evidence for the retained-feature model, or a limiting form of the full model? Clarifying that definition would help determine the appropriate treatment of pruned features.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import ARDRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
X = rng.normal(size=(12, 4))
y = X @ np.array([1.2, -0.5, 0.0, 0.8]) + rng.normal(
    scale=0.3, size=12
)

reg = ARDRegression(
    max_iter=1,
    compute_score=True,
    fit_intercept=False,
    threshold_lambda=1e12,
    alpha_1=0.2,
    alpha_2=0.3,
    lambda_1=0.7,
    lambda_2=1.2,
).fit(X, y)

alpha, lam = reg.alpha_, reg.lambda_
A = np.diag(lam) + alpha * (X.T @ X)
mu = alpha * np.linalg.solve(A, X.T @ y)
sse = np.sum((y - X @ mu) ** 2)

score_at_fitted_parameters = (
    (reg.lambda_1 * np.log(lam) - reg.lambda_2 * lam).sum()
    + reg.alpha_1 * np.log(alpha)
    - reg.alpha_2 * alpha
    + 0.5 * (
        -np.linalg.slogdet(A)[1]
        + X.shape[0] * np.log(alpha)
        + np.log(lam).sum()
        - alpha * sse
        - np.sum(lam * mu**2)
    )
)

print(reg.scores_[-1])
print(score_at_fitted_parameters)
```

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, this prints approximately `-5.488435` and `-7.335993`. No features are pruned in this example. The calculations use the same unnormalized objective, so omitted constants do not explain the difference.

### Expected Results

The final `scores_` entry should equal the objective evaluated at the fitted `alpha_` and `lambda_`. For this reproducer, that value is approximately `-7.335993011208482`. Each score should use the posterior and precisions from the same iteration.

### Actual Results

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, the reproducer prints:

```text
-5.48843505092349
-7.335993011208482
```

The first value is `reg.scores_[-1]`; the second is the objective recomputed at the fitted parameters. They differ by approximately `1.847558`.

### Versions

```shell
System:

executable: <local path>\Python314\python.exe

Python dependencies:

threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Built with OpenMP: True

    num_threads: 16

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes. I would be interested in working on a PR after the issue is triaged. The likely cause of the no-pruning discrepancy is that the score uses updated precisions with a posterior covariance and residual sum of squares computed before the update. I would make the score use a consistent parameter state and add a regression test for the reproducer. I would also confirm the intended objective after feature pruning with maintainers before changing that case.

title: BUG: trees `fit(..., check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`DecisionTree*.fit(X, y, check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values: with `check_input=False`, `_fit` skips `_compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask`, so `missing_values_in_feature_mask` stays `None` and the splitter treats NaNs as regular values. No error, no warning, just a wrong tree (NaN thresholds, spurious depth).

And there's no way around it from the public API: the mask can only be passed to the private `_fit`. That's what forests do (they compute the mask once and pass it to each tree via `tree._fit(..., check_input=False, missing_values_in_feature_mask=...)`).

Within scikit-learn, the only caller of the public `fit(..., check_input=False)` is `BaseGradientBoosting` (`_gb.py`), which is safe only because it rejects NaNs upfront. So this mostly affects third-party code using `check_input=False` (which the docstring discourages: "Don't use this parameter unless you know what you're doing").

More broadly, a single boolean isn't enough to express "this input was already validated" for trees anymore: callers also need to provide the missing-values mask (and, with categorical support, the encoding info). Possible ways forward:

1. **Compute the mask even when `check_input=False`** on the public `fit` (when none is provided). It's one pass over `X`, cheap compared to building a tree, and makes the result correct.
2. **Document** that missing values aren't supported with `check_input=False`. Cheap, but leaves a silent trap.
3. **Deprecate `check_input` in the public `fit`** of trees, and switch gradient boosting to `_fit` (like forests). With 1. applied during the deprecation cycle.

I'd go with 3.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [np.nan], [np.nan], [2.0], [3.0]], dtype=np.float32)
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])

for check_input in (True, False):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, y, check_input=check_input)
    print(f"{check_input=}: depth={tree.get_depth()}, thresholds={tree.tree_.threshold}")
```

### Expected Results

Same tree for both (or at least an error for `check_input=False`):

```
check_input=True: depth=1, thresholds=[inf -2. -2.]
```

### Actual Results

```
check_input=True: depth=1, thresholds=[inf -2. -2.]
check_input=False: depth=4, thresholds=[nan nan -2. -2. nan -2. nan nan -2. -2. -2.]
```

title: BUG: `BaggingClassifier` with feature sub-sampling fails when routing `X_val` to `HistGradientBoosting*`
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.


### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found while reviewing #34957.

`BaggingClassifier`/`BaggingRegressor` with `max_features < 1.0` (or `bootstrap_features=True`) fit each sub-estimator on `X[:, features]`, but they forward routed metadata as-is. So when `X_val` is routed to `HistGradientBoosting*`, the sub-estimator gets a full-width `X_val` while it was fitted on a subset of columns, and it raises:

```
ValueError: X has 20 features, but HistGradientBoostingClassifier is expecting 10 features as input.
```

The root cause is more general than Bagging: routers treat metadata as opaque, and only know how to slice "sample-aligned" metadata on rows (`_check_method_params`). They have no notion of "feature-aligned" metadata like `X_val`, which should get the same column selection as `X`. This seems closely related to #34270 (declaring metadata properties to be used by the routers).

With #34957, `X_val`/`y_val` will be auto-requested, so users will hit this more easily (no explicit `set_fit_request` needed).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=500, n_features=20, random_state=0)
X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val = X[:400], y[:400], X[400:], y[400:]

hgb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(early_stopping=True).set_fit_request(
    X_val=True, y_val=True
)
bagging = BaggingClassifier(hgb, max_features=0.5, random_state=0)
bagging.fit(X_train, y_train, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val)
```


### Expected Results


No error: each sub-estimator receives `X_val[:, features]`, i.e. the same feature subset as the `X` it's fitted on.

### Actual Results


<details>

```python-traceback
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 14, in <module>
    bagging.fit(X_train, y_train, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val)
  File "sklearn/base.py", line 1403, in wrapper
    return fit_method(estimator, *args, **kwargs)
  File "sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py", line 386, in fit

title: `from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises ImportError since 1.8.0
body:
### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm a CS student and regular scikit-learn user, mostly through model_selection. I ran into this while star-importing the module in a notebook and traced it back to a specific commit. First time filing a bug here.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises an ImportError on 1.8.0+. It worked in 1.7.2, and every other public submodule still star-imports fine.

The cause: `HalvingGridSearchCV` and `HalvingRandomSearchCV` are listed in `__all__` (in `sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py`), but the module's `__getattr__` deliberately raises ImportError for both until you import `enable_halving_search_cv`. Star-import pulls every name in `__all__`, so it hits that guard and fails. The two names were added to `__all__` in #31847 (the ruff absolute-imports cleanup); before that they weren't exported.

Impact: any notebook or script doing `from sklearn.model_selection import *` breaks on upgrade to 1.8.0, with an error that looks unrelated to what the user actually did.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import *
```

### Expected Results

Star-import succeeds like it did in 1.7.2, without exporting the experimental Halving classes.

### Actual Results

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py", line 100, in __getattr__
    raise ImportError(
ImportError: HalvingGridSearchCV is experimental and the API might change without any deprecation cycle. To use it, you need to explicitly import enable_halving_search_cv:
from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv
```

### Versions

```shell
System:

Also reproduces on 1.8.0.

title: DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

title: BUG: Explicit validation data does not enable HistGradientBoosting automatic early stopping
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

Keep `early_stopping=True` as a passing control. Additional coverage should preserve the sample-count rule when validation arrays are absent, including the 10,000-sample boundary, and preserve the existing validation-argument errors.

Related work: [#18748](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/18748) requested custom validation-set support, and [#27124](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27124) introduced the explicit validation arguments. These references do not establish that no duplicate report exists.

title: BUG: Pipeline.fit_predict skips transform_input for final-step metadata
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With metadata routing enabled and `transform_input=["X_val"]`, `Pipeline.fit_predict` passes transformed training data to the final estimator but leaves `X_val` untransformed. An otherwise identical call to `Pipeline.fit` transforms `X_val` correctly.

In the reproducer, the final estimator receives `X_val = [[15.0]]` through `fit_predict`, although the fitted scaler maps that value to `[[0.0]]`. No exception is raised.

This can put training data and validation metadata in different feature spaces. An estimator that uses the metadata could therefore compute incorrect validation quantities or make different fitting decisions. Preprocessing that changes the feature count could instead cause a shape error. These are potential consequences; the reproducer demonstrates the incorrect metadata, not a production failure or incorrect predictions from a built-in estimator.

The [documented purpose of `transform_input`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html) is to transform selected metadata before the consuming step receives it, including validation data.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)


class RecordsXVal(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        self.X_val_seen_ = X_val
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.zeros(len(X))

    def fit_predict(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.
author: Chaptyziok

title: BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data
body:
> [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```
### Expected Results Fitting on `X + offset` should not change `coef_` (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change `coef_` without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio (`X + ratio`, unit-variance `X`) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of `coef_` against the ratio=0 reference, for both `float32` and `float64`, with `×` marking points where a warning was raised: - `Ridge`, `LinearRegression`, `ElasticNet` (top two rows, the `_preprocess_data` family): error stays ~0 across the entire range, in both dtypes. A blip only appears in float32 at the extreme end (ratio ≥1e4), never in float64. - `LogisticRegression`, `TweedieRegressor`, `PoissonRegressor` (bottom three rows, the GLM family), with *either* solver (lbfgs or newton-cholesky): garbage coefficients starting at a ratio as low as ~20-100 in float32 and ~300-5000 in float64. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:23) [Clang 22.1.3 ] executable: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: None setuptools: None numpy: 2.5.3 scipy: 1.18.1 Cython: 3.3.0 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.6.0 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.26.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-f48b354e.so version: 0.3.34.106.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. title: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

### Expected Results

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

### Actual Results

```
1.9.1
importances_mean (max_samples=0.5): [ 1.7655429  -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):
[[-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
 [-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]]
importances_mean (max_samples=1.0): [1.79471992 0.         0.        ]
baseline (all rows) r2: 0.9095261981105188
max_samples=0.2: importances_mean = [ 1.76648851 -0.02631336 -0.02631336]  importances_std = [0.30605997 0.         0.        ]
max_samples=0.1: importances_mean = [1.66914758 0.00620688 0.00620688]  importances_std = [0.73546823 0.         0.        ]
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.14.7 (main, Aug  5 2026, 10:29:49) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
executable: /Users/luca/Projects/oss-contrib/.venv-skl/bin/python
   machine: macOS-26.6.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
          pip: 26.2.1
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.3
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd be willing to fix this. Idea: draw a fresh subsample for every repetition, and compute both the baseline and the shuffled scores on the same subsampled rows before subtracting. Add a regression test asserting that features the model does not use have exactly 0 importance when `max_samples < 1`.

title: DOC/ENH: StandardScaler silently sets scale to 1.0 for zero-variance features with no warning
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a recent CS/AI graduate currently building a personal finance app that uses scikit-learn for some ML-based features (budgeting insights, basic predictive modeling). While setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, I was testing edge cases with StandardScaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. I dug into the source (_handle_zeros_in_scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it.

I'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised
​```

This could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row
fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline —
producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something
unusual happened.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. This would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.

title: RFC CPU oversaturation/oversubscription due to third-party libraries when running containers on Linux
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Background

This is the result of a discussion with @ogrisel and @jeremiedbb, fleshed out and with some additional ideas. I make my suggestion at the end, but will require feedback before I do any of the work.

### The problem

When using a container on Linux (Docker, Kubernetes, anything using cgroups), you can set a CPU quota, something like "this process gets 2 cores worth of compute."

Unfortunately, not all third-party C libraries know this. At minimum OpenBLAS does not seem to know about this limit (). So if you have 64 core machine, and run a Kubernetes pod with 8 cores, and OpenBLAS will think it has 64 cores, and it will be much much slower. Similarly libgomp and libomp. MKL builds on OpenMP so maybe no point in filing there until libgomp/libomp are fixed.

* https://github.com/OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS/issues/6059
* https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=127651
* https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/225493

This is a performance problem for scikit-lean users.

### Demonstration

My CPU has 12 cores. I set up a cgroup with equivalent of 2 cores, but OpenBLAS still reports 12 cores:

```
$ systemd-run --user --scope --property CPUQuota="200%" -- python -c "import threadpoolctl; import numpy; print(threadpoolctl.ThreadpoolController().lib_controllers[0].get_num_threads())"
12
```

### Potential fixes

I am going to be fixing one case as a side-effect of https://github.com/joblib/joblib/issues/1846: when using `joblib.Parallel`, the number of cores will be constrained using `threadpoolctl`, including in sequential cases. However, this is a strange fix where if you don't use `joblib`, you still have the same performance problem.

So what else can be done until OpenBLAS any other relevant libraries fix this issue?

#### Option 1: joblib or scikit-learn set the limit correctly, on import

Instead of doing this in `Parallel` in the sequential case, do it on import of `joblib` or maybe `sklearn`: `threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))`.  (Technically this won't fix the above example because of https://github.com/joblib/loky/issues/634 but it will work in Docker or Kubernetes, and everywhere once that issue is fixed).

Pros:

* Fixes the limit for all use cases.

Cons:

* Importing a library changing global configuration. This is not very nice.

#### Option 2: sklearn sets the limit whenever calling into OpenMP or OpenBLAS

Pros:

* If you do `with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))` it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a _permanent_ global config change, it's just DTRT.

Cons:

* This adds performance overhead of all these calls.
* Lots of code changes.

#### Option 3: Documentation of the problem and how to solve it

Pros:

* No impacts on global behavior.

Cons:

* Most people won't notice the documentation.
* If the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs.

#### Option 4: Warn on import

If `os.process_cpu_count() > joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1)` then that means cgroups is restricting CPU count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. In practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail.

Pros:

* More likely to be noticed than docs.

Cons:

* Users will still have to do work.

### My suggestion

After further thought, I think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. The hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries DTRT, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do.

If that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what I would suggest doing.

I can proceed with either, once there is some consensus.

title: GaussianRandomProjection and SparseRandomProjection with n_components="auto" break get_feature_names_out and pandas output
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

`BaseRandomProjection.fit` ends with `self._n_features_out = self.n_components`. With the default `n_components="auto"` this stores the string `"auto"` instead of the inferred `n_components_`. As a result `get_feature_names_out` raises `TypeError` and `set_output(transform="pandas")` fails inside `fit_transform` for both `GaussianRandomProjection` and `SparseRandomProjection`.

The common estimator checks do not catch this because they force `n_components=2` on both classes, and `test_random_projection_feature_names_out` also uses `n_components=2`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.random_projection import GaussianRandomProjection

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 1000)
rp = GaussianRandomProjection(eps=0.5).fit(X)
print(rp.n_components_, repr(rp._n_features_out))
rp.get_feature_names_out()
```

The same happens with `SparseRandomProjection`, and with `rp.set_output(transform="pandas").fit_transform(X)`.

### Expected Results

110 feature names `gaussianrandomprojection0` to `gaussianrandomprojection109`, and a DataFrame with 110 columns when pandas output is requested.

### Actual Results

```
110 'auto'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../sklearn/base.py", line 1064, in get_feature_names_out
    return _generate_get_feature_names_out(
  File ".../sklearn/utils/validation.py", line 2471, in _generate_get_feature_names_out
    [f"{estimator_name}{i}" for i in range(n_features_out)], dtype=object
TypeError: 'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer

title: Clarify parameter/hyperparameter terminology in the cross-validation workflow diagram
body:
### Introduce yourself

I teach machine learning engineering to people who are new to machine learning.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

I use `GridSearchCV` to help learners understand grid search, model selection, and good practice. I think it is a fantastic teaching tool, and the user guide is excellent.

I've taught this section several times and have repeatedly needed to explain why the diagram says "parameters" when we are discussing hyperparameters. This is a recurring point of confusion in my teaching, which prompted this issue.

The overall workflow diagram in the cross-validation user guide uses the labels **"Parameters"** and **"Best parameters"**.

User guide:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html

Direct link to the diagram:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_images/grid_search_workflow.png

My learners are meeting the terms "parameter" and "hyperparameter" for the first time. They are still learning the difference between settings we specify or search over, such as a decision tree's maximum depth, and values the model learns during fitting.

When I explain grid search, I describe it as comparing hyperparameter settings. The diagram calls these "Parameters" and "Best parameters". I then have to explain why the same settings are being called by two different names, while learners are still trying to understand what those names mean.

I understand that scikit-learn uses "parameters" for estimator constructor settings. The glossary explains this convention:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The cross-validation guide also uses the word "hyperparameters". A short explanation at the diagram would help beginners connect the two terms.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Could a short note be added beside or below the diagram to explain how "parameters" relates to "hyperparameters"? For example:

> Here, "parameters" means configurable estimator settings. These can include machine-learning hyperparameters, such as a decision tree's `max_depth`, as well as other configuration choices, such as which estimator or pipeline step to use. They are different from values learned by the model during fitting.

The note could link to the glossary:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The diagram could keep its existing labels. The note would help beginners understand why settings such as `max_depth` may be called "hyperparameters" in machine-learning terminology while scikit-learn uses the broader term "parameters".

title: BUG fetch_file(url, folder=...) crashes with confusing FileNotFoundError instead of creating the directory
body:
### Describe the bug

`sklearn.datasets.fetch_file(url, folder=...)` raises a confusing, low-level `FileNotFoundError` instead of creating the target directory when the caller passes an explicit `folder` that doesn't exist yet.

The docstring for `folder` doesn't state that the directory must already exist:

> `folder` : str or Path, default=None
> Directory to save the file to. If None, the file is downloaded in a folder with a name derived from the URL host name and path under scikit-learn data home folder.

But directory creation only happens for the *default* case:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/datasets/_base.py#L1639-L1642

```python
if folder is None:
    folder = Path(get_data_home()) / folder_from_url
    makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
```

`makedirs(..., exist_ok=True)` is nested inside `if folder is None:`, so it only runs when `fetch_file` derives the folder itself. When the caller explicitly passes `folder=`, no directory creation happens at all. Downstream, `_fetch_remote` (same file, around line 1502) does:

```python
temp_file = NamedTemporaryFile(
    prefix=remote.filename + ".part_", dir=folder_path, delete=False
)
```

which raises `FileNotFoundError` if `folder_path` doesn't exist — an opaque, low-level crash referencing an internal `.part_...` temp-file name that the user never specified, rather than a clear message about the missing directory.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_file

# Using a local file:// URL as the "remote" source, no network required.
src_file = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "source.csv"
src_file.write_text("a,b,c\n1,2,3\n")
url = "file://localhost" + str(src_file)

target_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "does_not_exist_yet"
print("target_dir exists before:", target_dir.exists())

fetch_file(url, folder=target_dir)
```

### Expected Results

Either the directory gets created (matching what already happens for the default `folder=None` case — verified working), or a clear, actionable error naming the missing directory.

For comparison, the default-folder path already creates the directory transparently and succeeds:
```python
result = fetch_file(url)  # folder=None (default)
print(result, result.exists())  # succeeds, directory auto-created
```

### Actual Results

```
target_dir exists before: False
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/.../does_not_exist_yet/source.csv.part_1flw14k2'
```

### Versions

Reproduced on current `main`, no network access required (repro uses a local `file://` URL). This appears to have existed since `fetch_file` was introduced (#29354) — no prior discussion of this specific asymmetry found.

---

I dug into this while looking for an unrelated fix and haven't opened a PR — the obvious fix is to move (or duplicate) the `makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)` call so it also runs for a caller-supplied `folder`, mirroring the default-path behavior. Happy to put a PR together if that direction looks right to a maintainer.

title: BUG confusion_matrix_at_thresholds / roc_auc_score lose precision on plain numpy when y_score is float32 (regression from #34817)
body:
### Describe the bug

`confusion_matrix_at_thresholds` (and everything built on it: `roc_curve`, `precision_recall_curve`, `det_curve`, `roc_auc_score`) silently loses integer precision on **plain numpy** — not just the restricted array-API devices that #34817 was fixing — whenever the caller's `y_score` array is `float32`. Model scores/predictions are very commonly stored as `float32` (e.g. to save memory), so this is not an exotic input.

This looks like a regression introduced this week by #34817 (merged 2026-08-31), which switched the unweighted cumulative-sum path to compute exact `int64` counts and then cast them to `output_dtype`:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py#L1028-L1039

```python
y_true_int = xp.astype(y_true, xp.int64)
tps_int = xp.cumulative_sum(y_true_int, dtype=xp.int64)[threshold_idxs]
fps_int = (xp.astype(threshold_idxs, xp.int64) + 1) - tps_int

output_dtype = (
    y_score.dtype
    if hasattr(y_score, "dtype") and xp.isdtype(y_score.dtype, "real floating")
    else _max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)
)
tps = xp.astype(tps_int, output_dtype)
fps = xp.astype(fps_int, output_dtype)
```

`output_dtype` is set to `y_score.dtype` whenever `y_score` is real-floating, instead of the device's max-precision float dtype (`_max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)`, which is always `float64` on plain numpy). So on ordinary numpy — where `float64` is always available — if `y_score` happens to be `float32`, the exact `int64` counts get needlessly downcast to `float32`, which cannot represent integers exactly above 2**24 (~16.7M). The weighted branch right below doesn't have this problem: it always uses `max_float_dtype` regardless of `y_score`'s dtype.

This is exactly the precision-loss bug class #34817/#34813 set out to fix, just reintroduced on the ordinary numpy path whenever the *input* `y_score` happens to be float32 — a case the fix's own test suite doesn't cover (the added test `test_confusion_matrix_at_thresholds_float32_only_unweighted_large_n` only exercises the `array_api_strict` "no float64" restricted-device scenario, not plain numpy with a float32 `y_score`).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix_at_thresholds, roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 20_000_000
y_true = (rng.rand(n) < 0.9).astype(np.int32)
y_score64 = rng.rand(n).astype(np.float64)
y_score32 = y_score64.astype(np.float32)  # e.g. model scores stored as float32

_, _, _, tps64, _ = confusion_matrix_at_thresholds(y_true, y_score64)
_, _, _, tps32, _ = confusion_matrix_at_thresholds(y_true, y_score32)

print("tps64 dtype:", tps64.dtype, "last value:", tps64[-1])
print("tps32 dtype:", tps32.dtype, "last value:", tps32[-1])
print("n_pos (exact):", y_true.sum())

print("roc_auc_score (float64 y_score):", roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score64))
print("roc_auc_score (float32 y_score):", roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score32))
```

### Expected Results

`tps` should be exact regardless of `y_score`'s dtype, on a device where `float64` is available (matching the weighted branch's behavior, and matching pre-#34817 behavior):

```
tps64 dtype: float64 last value: 18000923.0
tps32 dtype: float64 last value: 18000923.0
n_pos (exact): 18000923
```

### Actual Results

```
tps64 dtype: float64 last value: 18000923.0
tps32 dtype: float32 last value: 18000924.0
n_pos (exact): 18000923
roc_auc_score (float64 y_score): 0.500012352595143
roc_auc_score (float32 y_score): 0.5000123248180354
```

The `float32`-`y_score` run silently gives a wrong (off-by-one, and for larger `n` increasingly wrong) true-positive count and a slightly different `roc_auc_score`, purely because of `y_score`'s dtype — with no warning and no restricted-device context involved.

### Versions

Reproduced on current `main` (post-#34817, i.e. including the fix for #34813/#34827) with plain numpy — no `array_api_dispatch` context, no array-API device involved.

---

I dug into this while looking for an unrelated fix and haven't opened a PR — happy to put one together (the obvious fix is to use `_max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)` unconditionally for `output_dtype`, mirroring the weighted branch, since it's already computed as the fallback) if that direction looks right to a maintainer.

title: Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hello,

I am facing a problem where the proper handling of infinite values would be helpful. Since the introduction of the support for missing values (#23595/#26391/#27966), I was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those.

Currently:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [np.inf], [10.0]])
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float32').
```

This is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in `BaseDecisionTree._compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask` (`sklearn/tree/_classes.py`):
A second guard in `_validate_X_predict` (same file) does the same at predict time.

```
if not np.isfinite(overall_sum):
    # Raise a ValueError in case of the presence of an infinite element.
    _assert_all_finite_element_wise(X, xp=np, allow_nan=True, **common_kwargs)
```

Both guards live on `BaseDecisionTree`, shared by all four tree classes; `RandomForest*`/`ExtraTrees*` call the same method rather than duplicating it. 

`GradientBoostingClassifier`/`Regressor` don't set `allow_nan` and aren't affected either way. Small number of call sites.

### Describe your proposed solution

The splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. Unlike NaN, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like NaN required. Verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: DecisionTreeClassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. Checked sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature_values[p_prev]/2.0 + feature_values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature_values[p_prev] if the result lands exactly on +INFINITY/-INFINITY. With real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too).

check_estimators_nan_inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow_nan tag covering both NaN and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. Proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow_nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/NaN test coverage.
author: lcrmorin

title: Add support for NumPy `StringDType`
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`numpy.dtypes.StringDType` (and other new-style DType classes) crash `xp.isdtype()` across many sklearn utilities.

`numpy`'s (and array-api-compat's) `isdtype()` raises `TypeError` instead of returning `False` for numpy's new-style DType classes. sklearn calls `xp.isdtype(...)` in many places expecting `False` for unrecognized dtypes, not a crash.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
np.isdtype(np.dtypes.StringDType(), "numeric")
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

```python
from sklearn.utils.multiclass import type_of_target
type_of_target(np.array(["a", "b", "a"], dtype=np.dtypes.StringDType()))
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

Confirmed crash sites (14), all via `xp.isdtype()` except `unique_labels`:

| Function | File |
|---|---|
| `check_array` (any `dtype=`, incl. `None`) | `utils/validation.py` |
| `type_of_target` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_is_integral_float` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_assert_all_finite` | `utils/validation.py` |
| `_randomized_range_finder` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_safe_accumulator_op` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_find_matching_floating_dtype` | `utils/_array_api.py` |
| `_average` | `utils/_array_api.py` |
| `label_binarize` | `preprocessing/_label.py` |
| `LabelBinarizer.inverse_transform` | `preprocessing/_label.py` |
| `RidgeClassifier.fit` | `linear_model/_ridge.py` |
| `_encode` | `utils/_encode.py` |
| `_check_unknown` (→ `OrdinalEncoder.fit_transform`) | `utils/_encode.py` |
| `unique_labels` (`np.dtype(y.dtype, metadata=...)`) | `utils/_unique.py` |

Not affected: `is_multilabel`, `LabelEncoder.fit`, `_array_indexing`, `_determine_key_type`.

Related: #34383 (motivation — proposes `StringDType` internally in encoders), #9777 (same failure pattern, closed).

### Expected Results

Unrecognized dtypes should be treated like any other unsupported dtype (e.g. return `False`/`"unknown"`), not raise.

### Actual Results

`TypeError` at every site listed above (`unique_labels` raises via a different call, same root cause).

### Versions

```shell
Python 3.11.15
scikit-learn 1.8.0 and 1.9.1 (both confirmed broken)
numpy 2.4.4
pandas 3.0.2
polars 1.44.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

One internal helper, e.g. `_safe_isdtype()`, wrapping `xp.isdtype()` to catch `TypeError` and return `False`, used at all sites above instead of patching each individually.
