title: Add Population Stability Index (PSI) as a model/data drift metric
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I want to detect when a feature's or a model score's distribution has shifted between two datasets (e.g. training vs. a more recent production sample). Using Population Stability Index - sum((new_pct - base_pct) * log(new_pct / base_pct)) over aligned bins/categories is a standard for doing so. 

This is one of the most common "has my model gone stale" checks in production ML monitoring, sitting next to sklearn.metrics conceptually (it's a distance/divergence metric between two empirical distributions, similar in spirit to things like scipy.stats.entropy/KL divergence that sklearn already depends on via scipy).

### Describe your proposed solution

sklearn.metrics.population_stability_index(base, new, bins=10) for continuous input (auto-binning via quantiles of base) and direct category alignment for categorical/discrete input, returning the scalar PSI (and optionally a per-bin breakdown table).

possibly also some rolling_psi method for evaluating the PSI over different time periods.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Checked scikit-learn's and statsmodels' issue trackers directly for prior discussion of PSI - found none in either (no open request, nothing closed as wontfix). Purpose-built alternatives exist as separate packages, but nothing really maintained, while PSI is old and widely used operationally.

### Additional context

Population Stability Index has been standard practice in credit scoring model monitoring since well before modern ML tooling (commonly attributed to the SAS/banking scorecard literature from the 1990s-2000s); today it's also used more broadly for feature/data drift detection outside credit scoring specifically.

title: Add Information Value (IV) / Weight-of-Evidence binning as metric and feature-selection
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.


### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Rank a feature's predictive strength against a binary target by binning it (equal-frequency or optimized) and computing Information Value: `sum((pct_event - pct_nonevent) * log(pct_event / pct_nonevent))` over bins.

This is a standard univariate feature-screening step in binary classification, conceptually adjacent to things sklearn already ships in `sklearn.feature_selection` (`mutual_info_classif`, `f_classif`, chi2) as a way to rank/filter features before modeling. Notably this metric does not depends on imbalance. 

### Describe your proposed solution

'sklearn.metric.IV(X,y, bins=10) would be useful for establishing Information value. Then 'sklearn.feature_selection.information_value(X, y, bins=10)' returning per-feature IV, using equal-frequency quantile binning by default (fast, matches the common textbook definition).


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Checked scikit-learn's issue tracker for "Information Value" and "Weight of Evidence" - found nothing (no open request, no closed-as-declined). The realistic existing option is `optbinning`, a purpose-built, actively maintained package that solves actual bin optimization (via a CP/MIP solver) rather than plain quantile cuts.

IV/WOE binning is old and widely used, but specifically within credit-scoring-style binary classification rather than general ML - similar concern to the adjacent PSI request I'm also filing. Raising it mainly to get a maintainer judgment on record, since I couldn't find this discussed anywhere in scikit-learn's history.



### Additional context

`mutual_info_classif` already covers "how predictive is this feature" in a distribution-agnostic way; IV specifically gives interpretable, additive-across-bins output that credit-risk practitioners rely on for regulatory model documentation, which is the main reason it persists as a distinct metric rather than being subsumed by mutual information in that field.

title: [BUG] RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None) returns incorrect best_score_ for binary classification
body:
### Introduce yourself

hello, I am a professor of computer science and a core developer at [aeon ](https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon). We use RidgeClassifierCV as a classifier head for many of our transformation based pipelines and ensembles, particularly the convolution based ones, and this bug was found by our core dev Matthew (@MatthewMiddlehurst) when reviewing [this PR] (https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon/pull/3655) that adapted one of these pipeline classifiers, the Arsenal, which is a component of our HIVE-COTEv2 classifier and is one of my finest moments in algorithm naming :) 

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None)` computes an incorrect best_score_ for binary classification problems: it always returns accuracy of 1.0, even when the problem contains substantial label noise and the fitted classifier is clearly not perfect.

We use best_score_ as an estimate of each ensemble member's classification accuracy and use it as an ensemble weight. For multiclass problems this appears to work as expected. For binary problems, however, all ensemble members receive a weight of 1.0, effectively disabling the weighting mechanism.

The behaviour appears specific to the default cv=None path. Using an explicit cross-validation splitter such as cv=5 gives plausible accuracy scores.

Looking at the implementation, the cause may be the classification scoring code in the GCV path reconstructing class labels using `y.argmax(axis=1)`. For binary classification, LabelBinarizer produces a single-column target, so argmax(axis=1) is always zero.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifierCV
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 20))
y = rng.randint(0, 2, size=200)

clf_loo = RidgeClassifierCV( alphas=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], scoring="accuracy", ).fit(X, y)
clf_cv = RidgeClassifierCV( alphas=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], scoring="accuracy", cv=5, ).fit(X, y)
print("cv=None best_score_:", clf_loo.best_score_)
print("cv=5 best_score_:", clf_cv.best_score_)
print("training accuracy:", clf_loo.score(X, y))

import sklearn;
sklearn.show_versions()
```
Outputs
```python
cv=None best_score_: 1.0
cv=5 best_score_: 0.515
training accuracy: 0.65
```
on random data. 

### Expected Results

an estimate of accuracy specific to the training data, not always 1.0.

chatgpt traced this back and thinks it was introduced in 0.23 by PR #14848, merged on 6 January 2020. I have not verified this myself.

### Actual Results

For binary classification with cv=None, best_score_ is always reported as 1.0

title: PolynomialCountSketch.bitHash_ docstring says dtype=float32 but is actually int64
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I found this while cross-checking
the `PolynomialCountSketch` docs against its implementation for an unrelated
performance PR (#34919) and noticed the `bitHash_` attribute's documented
dtype doesn't match what the code actually produces.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`PolynomialCountSketch`'s `bitHash_` attribute is documented as:

```
bitHash_ : ndarray of shape (degree, n_features), dtype=float32
    Array with random entries in {+1, -1}, used to represent
    the 2-wise independent hash functions for Count Sketch computation.
```

but it is actually set with:

```python
self.bitHash_ = random_state.choice(a=[-1, 1], size=(self.degree, n_features))
```

`numpy.random.RandomState.choice` with an integer array `a=[-1, 1]` and no
explicit `dtype` produces an integer array, not `float32`. This has been the
case since the class was introduced (scikit-learn/scikit-learn#13003, 2019),
so it is not a regression, just a docstring that was never accurate.

User-facing impact is limited (the attribute is internal-ish and the class
still works correctly), but anyone relying on the documented dtype — for
example writing code that assumes `bitHash_.astype(np.float32, copy=False)`
is a no-op, or reasoning about memory usage from the docstring — would be
misled.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import PolynomialCountSketch

X = np.random.RandomState(0).random_sample((50, 20))
ps = PolynomialCountSketch(degree=2, n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print(ps.bitHash_.dtype)
```

### Expected Results

```
float32
```
(matching the docstring)

### Actual Results

```
int64
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.14.6 (v3.14.6:c63aec69bd5, Jun 10 2026, 08:07:54) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
executable: /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/bin/python3
   machine: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
          pip: 26.1.2
   setuptools: 83.0.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: 3.3.0
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.25.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

I'd be happy to open a PR to fix the docstring to say the actual dtype
(`int64`, or more precisely whatever `numpy.random.RandomState.choice`
returns for an integer input array) once this is triaged.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I found this while looking for a
small contribution to make: the open issue backlog was heavily claimed
already, so I read through some less-trafficked modules directly and found
this in `kernel_approximation.py`.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`PolynomialCountSketch.transform`'s sparse-input branch loops over every
feature *and* every degree, slicing a single sparse column and densifying it
with `.toarray()` on each iteration:

```python
for j in range(X_gamma.shape[1]):
    for d in range(self.degree):
        iHashIndex = self.indexHash_[d, j]
        iHashBit = self.bitHash_[d, j]
        count_sketches[:, d, iHashIndex] += (
            (iHashBit * X_gamma[:, [j]]).toarray().ravel()
        )
```

This means the cost scales with `n_features * degree`, not with the number of
actual nonzeros, so a sparse matrix with a large number of columns but very
few nonzeros per column is transformed much slower than an equivalent dense
array of the same shape — defeating the purpose of the sparse code path. This
affects anyone using `PolynomialCountSketch` on sparse, wide, high-dimensional
data (e.g. bag-of-words or one-hot encoded features), where sparse support is
the main reason to reach for this transformer in the first place.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import PolynomialCountSketch

n_samples, n_components = 2000, 300
for n_features in [1000, 4000, 8000]:
    X_sparse = sp.random(n_samples, n_features, density=0.01, format="csc", random_state=0)
    X_dense = X_sparse.toarray()

    ps_sparse = PolynomialCountSketch(degree=2, n_components=n_components, random_state=0).fit(X_sparse)
    t0 = time.time()
    ps_sparse.transform(X_sparse)
    t1 = time.time()

    ps_dense = PolynomialCountSketch(degree=2, n_components=n_components, random_state=0).fit(X_dense)
    t2 = time.time()
    ps_dense.transform(X_dense)
    t3 = time.time()

    print(f"n_features={n_features} nnz={X_sparse.nnz} sparse={t1 - t0:.4f}s dense={t3 - t2:.4f}s")
```

### Expected Results

Transforming genuinely sparse input (1% density here) should be at least as
fast as transforming the equivalent densified array, since scipy sparse
operations scale with the number of nonzeros rather than the matrix shape.

### Actual Results

```
n_features=1000 nnz=20000  sparse=0.0970s dense=0.0151s
n_features=4000 nnz=80000  sparse=0.3228s dense=0.0380s
n_features=8000 nnz=160000 sparse=0.6310s dense=0.0690s
```

The sparse path is roughly 9-10x slower than the dense path on the same data
at every size tested, and the gap grows with `n_features` since the loop
count (not the nonzero count) drives the cost.

### Versions

```

```

(replacing the per-column densification with one sparse matrix
multiplication per degree) and will link the PR here once triage clears.

title: RFC Defining the auto-request strategy for scikit-learn estimators / sample_weight handling
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

_ACA Where do we want to use `sample_weight` by default?_

With #31413 ~~soon to be~~ merged, we have defined the mechanism for the auto-routing strategy in scikit-learn (and for use in third party libraries). It will be easily possible to define per estimator which methods of the estimator will request which metadata if users set `set_config(enable_metadata_requests=True)`. (Context: At one point in the future this setting will become the default, but for now it is opt-in.)

The way to do this is to call `add_auto_request` inside an estimator's `get_metadata_routing` method:

```py
class XYZEstimator(BaseEstimator):

    def get_metadata_routing(self):
        ...
        requests.fit.add_auto_request("sample_weight") # <--- one-liner to add auto-requests
        ...
```

The effect of adding an auto-request is that then `XYZEstimator.fit()` automatically requests and uses `sample_weight` if the user has passed it into the top-level meta-estimator or cross validation.

This issue is to define the scope of the auto-requests. 

We have discussed this in our bi-weekly meeting on pushing the subject of auto-requests and here we want to give everybody who is interested the opportunity to share their ideas on the following questions:

- Which metadata should get auto-requested ("sample_weigh", "X_val", "sample_weight_val", custom metadata, other?)
- Should we add auto-requests to `fit` and `score` everywhere or are there estimators where that doesn't make any sense?
- Which type of tests do we need?

My personal take would be to work these questions out in separate POC PRs.

CC @scikit-learn/core-devs for gathering opinions. I'm especially interested in the opinions of the statistically more inclined core devs (since we can figure out the engineering part pretty easily). Happy to discuss this in calls also.

title: Documentation: Incorrect description of statistic computed by MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Pradip, a Computer Engineering student and I’m currently learning and working with Python and machine learning. I use scikit-learn for learning and implementing machine learning algorithms and preprocessing techniques.

While going through the `MaxAbsScaler` documentation and source code, I noticed a discrepancy in the `partial_fit()` docstring. I’m opening this issue to clarify the documentation and make it consistent with the actual implementation.


### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` currently states that the data is used to compute the **"per-feature minimum and maximum"**.

However, `MaxAbsScaler` computes the **maximum absolute value** for each feature and stores it in `max_abs_`.

For example:

```python
X = [[-2, 5],
     [-3, 1]]
```

For the first feature:

```text
minimum = -3
maximum = -2
maximum absolute value = 3
```

`MaxAbsScaler` uses `3` as the scaling value. It does not use the minimum and maximum as separate statistics.

The implementation reflects this:

```python
max_abs = xpx.nanmax(xp.abs(X), axis=0, xp=xp)
```

Therefore, the current wording may confuse users into thinking that `MaxAbsScaler` computes and uses both the minimum and maximum values independently.

This also appears inconsistent with the class-level documentation, which describes the scaler in terms of the **maximum absolute value**.

I believe this is a documentation-only issue and does not require any change to the underlying algorithm.


### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I suggest updating the `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` from:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature minimum and maximum
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

to:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature maximum absolute value
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

This would make the `partial_fit()` documentation accurately reflect the statistic computed by the implementation and remain consistent with the class-level documentation.

title: balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the NaN filter
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a data scientist in Toronto working on forecasting and causal inference. I've recently started contributing to scikit-learn — I have an open PR at #34888 (array API support for ShrunkCovariance) — and I found this while looking into #33712, where I was trying to work out which of two distinct undefined cases in balanced_accuracy_score that issue refers to. This one turned out to be independent of it, so I'm filing it separately.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

balanced_accuracy_score(..., adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the internal NaN filter. The adjusted score is bounded — it spans [-1, 1], reaching -1 only at n_classes=2 — so -inf is outside the documented range of the metric.

This surfaces in cross-validation on small or imbalanced folds, where a fold can easily contain a single class. One -inf propagates through any mean over folds, turning the whole aggregate into -inf and silently destroying an otherwise valid CV score. The related nan case is at least absorbed by nan-aware aggregation; -inf is not.

Mechanism: n_classes is read after the NaN filter at _classification.py:2940, so when one class survives, chance = 1 / 1 and `score /= 1 - chance` at line 2946 divides by zero. The np.errstate guard wraps the per-class division only, not this one, and has been scoped that way since the original commit (e888c0d65cf, "ENH multiclass balanced accuracy" #10587, 2018) — the guard and the unguarded division were introduced together.

This is separate from #33712: it predates it and reproduces without touching replace_undefined_by.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

# Case 1
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], adjusted=True))

# Case 2
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], adjusted=True))
```

## Expected Results

A value within the documented range of the adjusted metric, [-1, 1]. A score documented as bounded should not return -inf.

## Actual Results

On scikit-learn 1.9.0 (installed from PyPI), case 1 returns nan:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:614: UserWarning: A single label was found in 'y_true' and 'y_pred'. For the confusion matrix to have the correct shape, use the 'labels' parameter to pass all known labels.
  warnings.warn(
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
nan
```

Case 2 returns -inf:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2939: UserWarning: y_pred contains classes not in y_true
  warnings.warn("y_pred contains classes not in y_true")
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: divide by zero encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
-inf
```

Both RuntimeWarnings come from the same unguarded statement at line 2946. The texts differ — "invalid value" for case 1, "divide by zero" for case 2 — which maps onto the nan/-inf split: case 1 is 0/0, case 2 is -0.333/0.

Also reproduces unchanged on main (1.10.dev0), where the filter is at line 2969 and the division at line 2975.

title: [BUG] `compute_class_weight` coerces class labels to int in 1.9, breaking dict lookup for string labels
body: ### Introduce yourself hi, I am a core developer for the aeon toolkit and an academic at the university of Southampton. I found this bug when trying to raise our upper bound for scikit https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon/pull/3787 For context, we have a range of algorithms that use scikit components, in this case the `ExtraTreeClassifier` and `RandomForestClassifier`. We also maintain a range of data archives including the UCR archive, hosted here http://timeseriesclassification.com/ Our classification data always loads class values as strings, so for example, "1"/"2" or "Run"/"Jump". The basic problem is that relevant parts of scikit 1.9 now always parse class value strings to integers, leading to dictionary errors. I had a good look and couldnt see this issue, sorry if its been fixed already. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In 1.9, fitting a forest ensemble with `class_weight="balanced"` raises `ValueError` when the class labels are strings that happen to parse as integers ("1", "2", ...). The same code works in 1.8 and earlier. Labels that are genuine integers, or strings that do not parse as integers ("a", "b"), are unaffected. The problem comes from a coercion added to the user-defined-dictionary branch of compute_class_weight in #32644 (commit 9ca766b, "FEA Add array API support for LogisticRegression with LBFGS"): ```python for i, c in enumerate(classes): try: c = int(c) except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings c = str(c) if c in class_weight: ``` The intent looks like normalising array scalars to Python scalars so that dict lookup by key works under a non-numpy namespace. But int("1") succeeds, so it never reaches the except clause that would have preserved the string. That branch is reached even though the user asked for "balanced", because `BaseForest._validate_y_class_weight` does not pass "balanced" straight through. It round-trips (sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py:861): ```python # Computing class_weight (dict or list) for the "balanced" option. class_weight_k_vect = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=self.classes_[k], ...) class_weight_k = {key: val for (key, val) in zip(self.classes_[k], class_weight_k_vect)} ... expanded_class_weight = compute_sample_weight(class_weight, y_original) ``` It first expands "balanced" into an explicit dict keyed by the original labels — {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, string keys — and then feeds that dict back in. The second call goes through the dictionary branch, the keys are coerced to int, every lookup fails, and all classes are reported as unweighted. Estimators that pass "balanced" directly to `compute_class_weight (DecisionTreeClassifier, RidgeClassifierCV, SVC, ...)` take the dedicated `elif class_weight == "balanced"` branch, which uses a LabelEncoder and never coerces, so they are not affected. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(20, 5) y = np.array(["1"] * 10 + ["2"] * 10) # string labels that parse as integers RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=5, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y) ```` Or against compute_class_weight directly, without the forest: ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight compute_class_weight( {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, classes=np.array(["1", "2"]), y=np.array(["1", "2", "1"]) ) ``` ### Expected Results Expected Results Fits without error, as in 1.8.0 and earlier. The direct compute_class_weight call returns array([1., 1.]). ### Actual Results ```python-traceback Traceback (most recent call last): File "repro.py", line 7, in RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=5, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y) File "sklearn/base.py", line 1403, in wrapper return fit_method(estimator, *args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py", line 393, in fit y, expanded_class_weight = self._validate_y_class_weight(y, sample_weight) File "sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py", line 879, in _validate_y_class_weight expanded_class_weight = compute_sample_weight(class_weight, y_original) File "sklearn/utils/_param_validation.py", line 191, in wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/utils/class_weight.py", line 236, in compute_sample_weight weight_k = compute_class_weight( File "sklearn/utils/_param_validation.py", line 191, in wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/utils/class_weight.py", line 117, in compute_class_weight raise ValueError( ValueError: The classes, [1, 2], are not in class_weight ``` The message is also misleading: it reports the classes as [1, 2] (post-coercion integers) when the real classes are the strings ["1", "2"], which are the dict keys. A mixed example shows the failure is per-label and driven purely by whether int() succeeds — with classes ["0", "a"] only "0" is reported: This effects both ExtraTreesClassifier and RandomForestClassifier ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.12.9 [MSC v.1942 64 bit (AMD64)] machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.9.0 pip: 26.1.2 setuptools: 82.0.1 numpy: 2.4.6 scipy: 1.18.0 Cython: None pandas: 2.2.3 matplotlib: 3.10.1 joblib: 1.4.2 threadpoolctl: 3.5.0 ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug yes I would be happy to, I would not convert strings to ints at all, leave them as string and would not use a try ... except block in this context and avoid the round trip, but would need to look more closely, claude suggests this fix (and has helped me pin this down) ```python Convert the labels to Python scalars without altering their values, rather than parsing them. move_to is already imported and used earlier in the same function: for i, c in enumerate(classes): - try: - c = int(c) - except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings - c = str(c) + # convert to python scalars so that lookup by dict key works for any + # array namespace, without altering the label values themselves + for i, c in enumerate(move_to(classes, xp=np, device="cpu").tolist()): if c in class_weight: tolist() maps each element to its natural Python type — str stays str, int stays int — and both hash-match the user's dict keys, which is what the array-API port needed. Unlike int(), it never alters a label's value, so it cannot introduce this class of mismatch for any label type. ``` A narrower guard such as if not isinstance(c, str) around the existing int() call also fixes it, which is probably what I would do, but I obviously dont have the wider picture.

title: SelectFromModel's `prefit` fails unless fit is called when set_output(transform="pandas")
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

My understanding is that if `prefit`is true, one could, in principle call `transform()` without calling `fit()` first.

While this is true if we don't set the output to pandas, it fails when we do so:

Minimal reproduction:

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel

X, y = load_iris(as_frame=True, return_X_y=True)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)

# prefit=True -- docs say we don't need to call .fit() on sel
sel = SelectFromModel(clf, prefit=True).set_output(transform="pandas")

sel.transform(X)
```

```
NotFittedError: This SelectFromModel instance is not fitted yet. Call 'fit' with appropriate arguments before using this estimator.
```

Without `.set_output(transform="pandas")`, the identical `prefit=True` selector transforms `X` just fine with no `.fit()` call. 

The error only appears once pandas output is requested, because `set_output` internally calls `get_feature_names_out()`, which checks whether the *wrapper itself* has been fitted (via `check_is_fitted(self)`, not `check_is_fitted(self.estimator)`). 

According to Claude, that check was intentionally added in #25308 to standardize `get_feature_names_out()` behavior across `SelectorMixin` estimators.

So my question is: is this expected behaviour? or is it an unintended bug? 

From a user perspective, if I use `fit`again, even though prefit is True, I get the impression that my estimator would be re-fitted, so if this is intended, it might be worth adding a line in the docs.

```python
sel.fit(X, y)     # with prefit=True, does NOT retrain clf -- just
                  # deep-copies it and records feature_names_in_
sel.transform(X)  # now works
```

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

SelectFromModel's prefit parameter is documented as:

prefit : bool, default=False
Whether a prefit model is expected to be passed into the constructor directly or not. If True, estimator must be a fitted estimator. If False, estimator is fitted and updated by calling fit and partial_fit, respectively.

Maybe it's just me, but I sort of read this as, if the estimator is prefit, I could avoid calling fit and it would be just fine.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a note to the prefit parameter docstring, e.g.:

Note: even with prefit=True, .fit() must still be called before using get_feature_names_out() or set_output(transform="pandas"), since these check whether the selector itself (not the underlying estimator) has been fitted. Calling .fit() in this case does not refit estimator; it only records bookkeeping metadata (estimator_, feature_names_in_).
author: solegalli

title: Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case)
body:
While looking at [builds comparison results](https://probabl-ai.github.io/scikit-learn-benchmarks/builds_comparison.html) from my benchmarks (https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks), I noticed `ExtraTrees*.fit` was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of
scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels.

Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown:

1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): `-O3` in meson doesn't survive an environment `CFLAGS` that also sets `-O2` (which conda-forge's compiler activation does).

2. **Version of `glibc`** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a `sysroot_linux-64=2.17` (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's `<math.h>` defines the `isnan()` macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal `__isnanf`/`__isnan` functions instead of `__builtin_isnan*`. GCC can't recognize or inline those, so `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx`'s `isnan(value)` calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (`find_min_max`, `partition_samples`) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is `fit`-specific (confirmed: `predict`, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned.


This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop `isnan()`/`isinf()` call is plausibly exposed the same way.

~~=> TODO: Open an issue in conda-forge~~ Done: I posted a comment here: https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock/issues/108

### Proposed fix

Replace `from libc.math cimport isnan` / `isnan(value)` in `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test `value != value`. Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever.

### Root cause, in detail

*(pure LLM write-up)*

<details>

`sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` (`DensePartitioner.find_min_max`, `.partition_samples`) and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` call `isnan(value)` on `float32_t` data, via `from libc.math cimport isnan`. This runs once per sample per feature scan during `fit`; never during `predict`.

The feedstock's CI pin file (`.ci_support/linux_64_python3.12.____cpython.yaml` at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets `c_stdlib: sysroot`, `c_stdlib_version: '2.17'`. That sysroot's `math.h` has:

```c
#  define isnan(x) \
     (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? __isnanf (x) \
      : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? __isnan (x) : __isnanl (x))
```

Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier `isnan` is gone from
the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so
`__isnanf` (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic)
gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines `isnan(x)` as
`__builtin_isnan(x)` directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions
(`ucomiss`/`setp`). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're
built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern
headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning*
at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers.

Confirmed end to end:
- `perf`-profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages
  (`ExtraTreesRegressor.fit`, `n_features=30`): conda-forge spends 12.6% of
  samples in `__isnanf` alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all.
- Disassembled both real `.so` files directly: conda-forge's
  `find_min_max` has `call *0x1791f(%rip)  # <__isnanf@GLIBC_2.2.5>`;
  PyPI's has no call at all.
- Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact
  matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own
  `.comment` section) reproduced nothing *until* `sysroot_linux-64=2.17`
  was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the
  latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the
  larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte.
- Same `isnan()` call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on
  current `main` (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added
  since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — `find_min_max` compiles to the
  identical byte size on both).

</details>

### Everything else that was tried and ruled out

Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge `gcc_linux-64`/`gxx_linux-64` toolchain:

<details>

- `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (~1.7% effect — this is the Meson bug above)
- `-march=nocona -mtune=haswell` vs no override
- GCC version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact `14.3.0-19` patch build
  (pinning `gcc_impl_linux-64`/`gxx_impl_linux-64`/`binutils_impl_linux-64`
  precisely, since `gcc_impl_linux-64` has its own build-number sequence
  independent of the `gcc_linux-64` wrapper)
- Cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up
  3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect)
- Exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current `main`
- Editable install vs literal `python -m build -w` wheel build (matching
  `build.sh` exactly)
- `-fno-merge-constants` (the extra flag conda-forge adds under
  `CONDA_BUILD=1`)
- joblib version, core-count detection, BLAS threading config — all
  identical between real PyPI and conda-forge installs

</details>

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'll open the PR very soon.

title: Investigation: Meson silently downgrades -O3 to -O2 under conda-forge CFLAGS
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Meson's `buildtype: release` implies `-O3` for every compiled extension in the project. Under conda-forge, it doesn't: conda-forge's compiler activation injects its own `-O2` via `CFLAGS`/`CXXFLAGS`, and Meson appends environment flags *after* its own optimization flag on the compiler command line. GCC/Clang use the **last** `-O` flag, so conda-forge's `-O2` silently wins:
```
cc ... -O3 ... -march=nocona -mtune=haswell ... -O2 -ffunction-sections -pipe ... -c foo.c
```



This was first noticed via `sklearn/tree/meson.build`'s `override_options: ['optimization=3']` (an explicit ask that's supposed to matter for `_splitter.pyx`/`_partitioner.pyx`'s branch-heavy loops) silently doing nothing under conda-forge, but that's just the one place the override was visible enough to check.

This is a known Meson/conda-forge interaction, not new: mesonbuild/meson#15055 (closed as docs — "CFLAGS in general tend to override buildtype flags, as they are appended") and conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock#157 (still open/unmerged for gcc/Linux).

**However: benchmarking `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (real conda-forge toolchain) did not show any observable performance effect on what I tried for now.**. Contrary to an other conda-forge compilation chain setting that does cause an important slowdown on `ExtraTrees*`, see: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34869

For now, I'm not sure we should bother fixing it. Claude had a way to fix it, see PR #34864 (but I closed it for now).

title: BUG: `QuantileTransformer()` sub-sampling impact is too high for sparse matrices
body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact Related to #34298 and #32585 For very sparse columns falling in the sub-sampling path, the number of actually sampled data will be `self.subsample * len(column_nnz_data) // n_samples`, which for the default `subsample=10_000` and 0.1% sparsity is 10... Which can quickly get noising. This can cause a lot of samples to collapse to 1 after fit-transform, distorting the output distribution weirdly. See the plot below. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```Python import numpy as np from scipy.sparse import csc_matrix from sklearn.preprocessing import QuantileTransformer import matplotlib.pyplot as plt subsample = 10_000 # default value qt = QuantileTransformer(subsample=subsample, random_state=2) # create a very sparse (0.1% sparsity) X matrix with one column: n, d = 10**7, 1 # set nnz to `subsample + 1` to use the sub-sampling code path: nnz = subsample + 1 X = csc_matrix(( np.random.RandomState(4).rand(nnz), (np.arange(nnz), np.zeros(nnz)) ), shape=(n, d)) plt.hist(qt.fit_transform(X).data, bins=100); ``` ### Expected Results ### Actual Results ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.12.3 (main, Jun 19 2026, 12:46:00) [GCC 13.3.0] executable: [/home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python](https://file+.vscode-resource.vscode-cdn.net/home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python) machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: 26.2.1 setuptools: 78.1.0 numpy: 2.5.1 scipy: 1.18.0 Cython: 3.2.8 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.5.3 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.24.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: [/home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-017048f4.so](https://file+.vscode-resource.vscode-cdn.net/home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-017048f4.so) version: 0.3.33.112.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: [/home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so](https://file+.vscode-resource.vscode-cdn.net/home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so) version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: [/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0](https://file+.vscode-resource.vscode-cdn.net/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0) version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I'm about to open a PR that fixes it.

title: BIC-based model selection in plot_gmm_selection.py silently picks the wrong model under anisotropy severe enough to break its own initialization
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

## Describe the issue linked to the documentation

`examples/mixture/plot_gmm_selection.py` demonstrates using `GridSearchCV` + BIC to select `n_components` and `covariance_type` for a `GaussianMixture`. It works well on the example's data because the two components are already well separated relative to their own spread, so `GaussianMixture`'s default k-means-style initialization lands close to the true partition and EM refines it correctly.

As in [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), that init dependency is invisible in the example and doesn't generalize. If the true clusters are anisotropic enough that Euclidean-distance-based initialization is already unreliable, BIC does not fail loudly -- it fails silently, by scoring every candidate in the grid on a bad fit and confidently reporting the best of a bad set. A reader walks away with "BIC picked `n_components=2`, full covariance, done" with no signal that a different initialization would have picked a different, better-scoring model entirely.

Concretely, on two anisotropic "parallel cigars" clusters (`make_blobs` + a linear `transformation`, same construction as [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), ratio 4x rather than 80x), the grid search over `n_components` and `covariance_type` with default initialization selects a 3-component model, when the true generative model has 2 components. The 2-component model is available in the same search space -- it's just never found, because every restart of k-means++ on this data lands in roughly the same wrong place.

## Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a new section to `plot_gmm_selection.py`, after the existing example, showing:

1. The same "parallel cigars" dataset as [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), where default (raw) k-means-style initialization for `GaussianMixture` gives a partition bad enough that BIC-based model selection lands on the wrong `n_components`.
2. A whitened-init variant: use `PCA(whiten=True)` + `KMeans` only to get an initial cluster assignment, derive `weights_init`/`means_init` from that assignment on the raw data, then fit and score every model (whitened-init or not) by BIC on the raw data. This keeps the BIC comparison valid while showing that whitening the initialization -- not the model itself -- restores the correct selection.

Draft implementation, for review before opening a PR: https://github.com/jovo/scikit-learn/pull/2 (this is a fork-internal PR against my own fork, not yet a real PR against `scikit-learn/scikit-learn` -- opening one once there's agreement this is worth doing, per the guidance on [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842)).

title: GaussianMixture is not a universal fix for anisotropy — plot_kmeans_assumptions.py doesn't show the case where whitening is needed too
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

`examples/cluster/plot_kmeans_assumptions.py` shows `KMeans` failing on anisotropic blobs and proposes `GaussianMixture` as the fix, since it fits a full covariance per component instead of assuming spherical clusters.

That's correct for the anisotropy shown in the example, but not universally: `GaussianMixture` is still initialized from a k-means-style partition of the raw data, and EM only ever *refines* that partition rather than searching from scratch. If the anisotropy is severe enough, the initial partition can already be too wrong for EM to recover from, even with unconstrained covariances.

**What a reader might do without knowing this:** someone hits poor `KMeans` results on their own anisotropic data, finds this example, and takes away the rule "if k-means struggles with anisotropy, switch to `GaussianMixture`." They swap it in, `GaussianMixture` returns *some* clustering with no error or warning, and they ship it — never realizing the result can be arbitrarily wrong, because their anisotropy happened to be severe enough to also break the initialization this fix silently depends on. Nothing in the current example signals that this failure mode exists, so there's no reason for them to suspect it.

I'd like to propose adding: a more severely anisotropic dataset (built the same way as the file's existing `X_aniso` — `make_blobs` + a linear `transformation`, just more extreme) where `GaussianMixture` fails (ARI ≈ 0), and where whitening first with `PCA(whiten=True)` fixes it (ARI ≈ 0.9+) — no custom clustering code needed, just a change of input to the same `GaussianMixture` call.

(Caveat: this degrades in high dimension too — same construction at d=30, ARI drops back to ≈0.)

Draft implementation, kept up to date: jovo/scikit-learn#1 (opened against my own fork so it stays open and reviewable rather than getting auto-closed like a direct PR here would while this issue is pending triage — happy to open a PR against this repo once there's agreement this is worth doing).
author: jovo

title: StratifiedGroupKFold returns an empty fold when n_groups == n_splits: least-populated-fold tiebreak is defeated by 1-ULP noise
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

`StratifiedGroupKFold` can return an empty test fold even when `n_groups >= n_splits`, because the "least populated fold" tiebreak in `_find_best_fold` is defeated by 1-ULP floating-point noise.

`_find_best_fold` selects a fold with:

```python
is_current_fold_better = fold_eval < min_eval or (
    np.isclose(fold_eval, min_eval)
    and samples_in_fold < min_samples_in_fold
)
```

The first branch uses an exact `<`. When two candidate folds are *mathematically* tied, `np.std` still returns values that differ by an ULP or two, so `fold_eval < min_eval` fires and that fold wins outright — the `samples_in_fold` comparison never runs. That comparison is the "heuristic for assigning group to the least populated fold in cases when all other criteria are equal" documented in the changelist comment at the top of `_iter_test_indices`, and in practice it is largely unreachable.

When `n_groups == n_splits` there is no slack: a single misdirected group leaves a fold with nothing in it.

This is distinct from #33085, which was about `n_groups < n_splits` and was addressed by #33176 (that PR was titled "Towards #33085" and the issue remains open).

**Impact.** `cross_val_score` silently produces `nan` for the empty fold, so the aggregate score becomes `nan`:

```python
scores: [0.6  0.375  nan  0.6]   ->  mean nan
```

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold

y = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0]  # 3 classes, 6 samples each
g = [0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 3, 3, 0, 2]  # 4 groups, sizes 5/3/2/8

for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=4).split(y, y, g)):
    print(f"fold {i}: n_train={len(tr):2d} n_test={len(te):2d}")
```

### Expected Results

Four non-empty test folds. With 4 groups and 4 splits the assignment is forced to one group per fold.

```
fold 0: n_train=16 n_test= 2
fold 1: n_train=15 n_test= 3
fold 2: n_train=13 n_test= 5
fold 3: n_train=10 n_test= 8
```

### Actual Results

```
fold 0: n_train=13 n_test= 5
fold 1: n_train=10 n_test= 8
fold 2: n_train=18 n_test= 0    <-- empty test fold
fold 3: n_train=13 n_test= 5
```

`shuffle` does not help: all 24 relabellings of the four groups, and all of `random_state=0..199` with `shuffle=True`, still produce an empty fold.

### Mechanism

Instrumenting the assignment loop, the second group is the decisive one:

```
-- group 1 counts=[0, 1, 2]
     fold 0: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 1: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 2: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 3: eval=0.12028130608117203  samples_before=2   <- 1 ULP lower
     -> chose fold 3
```

Three folds are empty, fold 3 already holds a group, and all four evaluations are mathematically identical. Fold 3 wins on a 1-ULP artefact, and fold 2 is never filled.

Measured over 15898 group-assignment decisions from randomised configurations:

- 7.0% of decisions have two or more mathematically tied folds whose winner is decided by floating-point noise (median deciding difference **1 ULP**, max 3).
- In 6.9% of all decisions the intended least-populated-fold tiebreak would have selected a *different* fold than the one actually chosen.

### Additional counterexamples

Found by random search; all reproduce identically on 1.9.0 and 1.10.dev0.

| `n_splits` | `n_groups` | `n` | fold sizes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 22 | `[6, 11, 0, 5]` |
| 6 | 6 | 24 | `[4, 6, 6, 0, 4, 4]` |
| 4 | 4 | 20 | `[4, 9, 0, 7]` |
| 5 | 5 | 13 | `[2, 3, 4, 0, 4]` |

Every failing case I found is at `n_groups == n_splits`; with one spare group I found none in ~25k configurations either way.

### Suggested fix

Require a strictly-better evaluation to be better by more than noise, so the tiebreak becomes reachable:

```python
is_tied = np.isclose(fold_eval, min_eval)
is_current_fold_better = (fold_eval < min_eval and not is_tied) or (
    is_tied and samples_in_fold < min_samples_in_fold
)
```

With that change the reproducer yields `[2, 3, 5, 8]`, and in a sweep of the sensitive regime (`n_splits` 2-6, `n_classes` 2-4, `n < 40`) empty folds go from **4/73401 to 0/73401**. `pytest --pyargs sklearn.model_selection` is unchanged at 642 passed / 238 skipped.

Two caveats worth discussing:

1. **It changes roughly 21% of splits.** That is the size of the latent defect rather than an over-aggressive tolerance: tightening `np.isclose` to `rtol=1e-9` or `1e-12` gives the same 21%, because these are true ties; exact equality drops churn to 0.3% but does not fix the bug.
2. **Stratification quality is essentially unchanged** — mean fold-size CV 0.2393 both ways, mean per-fold class-proportion deviation 0.10618 vs 0.10620 over 4000 configurations. This is a correctness fix for the degenerate case, not an improvement to stratification (cf. #24656).

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8]
   machine: macOS-26.6-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
        numpy: 2.6.0.dev0
        scipy: 2.0.0.dev0
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Also reproduced on released sklearn 1.9.0 with numpy 2.5.2 / scipy 1.18.1.
```

author: david-cortes-intel

title: OneHotEncoder unknown-category warning is incorrect for columns without an infrequent category
body:
### Introduce yourself

I'm learning ML engineering and use scikit-learn for a delay-prediction model on
US flight data. This is the first issue I've opened. I encountered this while working out how to encode categorical columns that may contain previously unseen values during prediction.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Carrier and destination can't be enumerated ahead of time, so both go to one
encoder with `drop="first"`, `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"` and
`min_frequency=4`. On my first CV fold, 41,901 rows, it fits to:

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['HDN'], dtype=object)]
```

Destination gets an infrequent bucket. Carrier gets `None` because its rarest value has 148 rows in that fold and 744 across the training pool, so it is not below `min_frequency=4`. Transforming a row with an unknown carrier and an unknown destination produces this warning:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown
categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

The warning claims that the unknown categories in both columns will go to the infrequent category, but this is not true for the carrier feature because no `infrequent_sklearn` column exists for it, and the transformed row is zero across the entire carrier block.

This matters because `drop="first"` drops the encoded feature for the first carrier category (`AA` in this fold), making all zeros its carrier encoding. An unknown airline and a real flight belonging to `AA` therefore produce an identical carrier encoding, so the model treats them the same with respect to the carrier feature.

I caught this by inspecting `infrequent_categories_`, transforming a row containing an unknown carrier and destination, and comparing the resulting vector with `get_feature_names_out()`. The carrier block was entirely zero, even though the warning said that the unknown carrier would be encoded as the infrequent category. The warning should have identified that the unknown carrier was encoded as all zeros, while the unknown destination was routed to its infrequent bucket.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import warnings

from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Column 0: "a" and "b" both appear twice, so it has no infrequent category.
# Column 1: "y" appears once, so it does have an infrequent category.
X = [["a", "x"], ["a", "x"], ["b", "x"], ["b", "y"]]

encoder = OneHotEncoder(
    drop="first",
    sparse_output=False,
    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
    min_frequency=2,
).fit(X)

print("infrequent_categories_:", encoder.infrequent_categories_)
print("feature names:         ", encoder.get_feature_names_out())

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    X_trans = encoder.transform([["c", "z"]])

print("transform([['c', 'z']]):", X_trans)
print("warning:", caught[0].message)
```

Both columns receive an unknown category, but only column 1 has an infrequent
category that can absorb it.


### Expected Results

The warning should describe what actually happens to each column. Column 1 has
an infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded there. Column 0 has
no infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded as all zeros, which is the same encoding `drop="first"` assigns to the dropped category.

Something along the lines of:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. The unknown
categories in columns [1] will be encoded as the infrequent category. Those in
columns [0] will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no
infrequent category.
```

This is also what the `handle_unknown` docstring already documents:

> If the `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then `transform` and
> `inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
> `handle_unknown='ignore'`.


### Actual Results

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['y'], dtype=object)]
feature names:          ['x0_b' 'x1_infrequent_sklearn']
transform([['c', 'z']]): [[0. 1.]]
warning: Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

No exception is raised. The problem is that the warning talks about both columns and
makes a single claim about them, which is false for column 0: its
`infrequent_categories_` entry is `None`, no `x0_infrequent_sklearn` column
exists in `get_feature_names_out()`, and the transformed row is `0` across the
whole column-0 block.

Also reproduced on main (1.10.dev0) at a456b324bc, with identical output.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8 ]
   machine: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
          pip: 25.2
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.2
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: 3.0.5
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.25.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in opening a PR if this is triaged as a bug.

The warning message is selected once from `handle_unknown`, but the actual outcome is determined separately for each column in `_map_infrequent_categories` (`sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`). I would update the warning to distinguish columns that have an infrequent category from those that fall back to all zeros, update the affected warning assertions, and add a regression test for the mixed case above.

title: Numerical stability of `confusion_matrix_at_thresholds` on `float32`-only capable array API devices
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

As discussed in #33200, `confusion_matrix_at_thresholds` currently relies on an upcast to `_max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)` which is `float64` for numpy on CPU and many array API devices for can be limitted to `float32` on common devices such as torch MPS (Apple GPUs) or some older Intel GPUs via torch XPI.

## Possible solution

I think this code could be changed to improve numerical stability (and maybe processing speed) by implementing either or both of the following two strategies:

### When `sample_weight is None`

Using an integer dtype to perform the call to `xp.cumulative_sum` instead and only after casting the results to the dtype of `y_score`.

### When `sample_weight is not None`

Remove the upcast to `_max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)` and instead compute the total weight sum and normalize the `weight` array before calling the cumulative sum. Here is the pseudo-code `tps = xp.cumulative_sum(y_true * weight / weigh.sum(), dtype=y_score.dtype) * weight.sum()`.

## Resolution plan

I think the first step is to do a quick empirical study on a float32 only device to confirm that this function actually has a numerical stability problem. Instead of MPS, we could leverage [array-api-strict's float32-only devices](https://github.com/data-apis/array-api-strict/pull/206) and call that function on arrays with a large number of elements to try to trigger the problem and then check that the proposed solution actually work as intended. If this is the case we could open two independent PRs, one for the weighted case and one for the unweighted case.

```shell
 - pytest-xdist: 3.8.0                                                                                    
 - OS: openSUSE Tumbleweed
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

## Description

The following scikit-learn test fails intermittently or consistently on i586 with Python 3.14.7:

```text
sklearn/callback/tests/test_callback_support.py::test_function_no_callback_support[RecordingCallback-processes-2]
```

The failure occurs only for the process-based case with `n_jobs=2`. The thread-based cases and the `n_jobs=1` case pass.

## Environment

- scikit-learn: 1.9.0
- Python: 3.14.7
- Architecture: i586
- joblib: 1.5.3
- pytest: 9.0.3
- pytest-xdist: 3.8.0
- OS: openSUSE Tumbleweed

## Reproduction

Run:

```bash
pytest -q sklearn/callback/tests/test_callback_support.py \
  -k 'test_function_no_callback_support'
```

The failing parameter combination is:

```text
test_function_no_callback_support[RecordingCallback-processes-2]
```

The relevant test code creates a callback-bearing estimator and sends it to process workers through joblib:

```python
callback = RecordingCallback()
estimator = MaxIterEstimator(max_iter=7).set_callbacks(callback)

Parallel(n_jobs=2, prefer="processes")(
    delayed(clone_and_fit)(estimator) for _ in range(5)
)
```

## Actual result

The test fails while joblib/cloudpickle serializes the task:

```text
RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration
when serializing dict item 'record'
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback state
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback object
```

This is then reported by joblib as:

```text
_pickle.PicklingError: Could not pickle the task to send it to the workers.
```

Full traceback excerpt:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../joblib/externals/loky/backend/queues.py", line 159, in _feed
    obj_ = dumps(obj, reducers=reducers)
  ...
  File ".../joblib/externals/cloudpickle/cloudpickle.py", line 1313, in dump
    return super().dump(obj)
RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration

when serializing dict item 'record'
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback state
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback object
```

## Expected result

The test should complete successfully, as it does for:

```text
RecordingCallback-threads-1
RecordingCallback-threads-2
RecordingCallback-processes-1
RecordingAutoPropagatedCallback-processes-2
```

## Analysis

`RecordingCallback` stores its records in a regular list:

```python
self.record = []
self._listener_handle = open_listener(self.record.append, owner=self)
```

When the worker processes execute the estimator, callback messages are sent back to the parent process. The listener thread appends those messages to `callback.record`.

At the same time, joblib/cloudpickle serializes the estimator and callback to send work to another process. This means that cloudpickle can be iterating over `callback.record` while the listener thread appends to it.

The failure appears to be a timing-dependent race between callback message handling and process-task serialization. It was observed on i586, where the slower execution may make the race easier to trigger. I have not determined whether this is caused by a Python 3.14 behavior change, or whether Python 3.14 merely exposes an existing race in the test or callback implementation.

Could this test or callback state be made safe to pickle while callback records are being received? For example, should the live recording state be excluded from the pickled state, synchronized during serialization, or otherwise handled specially?

body:

### Introduce yourself

I am saikrishna working as a senior data engineer I have bachelors degree in computer science with data analytics specialization where I have worked on wide variety of tools like numpy, pandas, scikit-learn,... Where i have done various projects using various tools. Now I was reading the source looking for a bug to fix, part of it while testing a piece of code i have come across this. So i wanted to contribute and help tool perform better.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

so the `split_sign=True` makes `transform` return `2 * n_components` columns and the rest of the class does not know this. A `DictionaryLearning(split_sign=True)` step inside a `Pipeline` fits without any issue initially and then raises at `predict`.

so this has 3 symptoms:
- `get_feature_names_out()` returns half the names
- `set_output(transform="pandas")` raises `Length mismatch`
- float32 input comes back as float64

This also affects all three sparse-coding transformers: `DictionaryLearning`, `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning`, `SparseCoder`.

Previous works: 
- #11000 already has DictionaryLearning and MiniBatchDictionaryLearning checked off as dtype-preserving.

- #32077 brought `SparseCoder` into the common tests and yet the float32 upcast survives in all the three because no common tests sets `split_sign=True`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import DictionaryLearning
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(60, 5) + 0.5
y = np.random.RandomState(1).rand(60)

dl = DictionaryLearning(n_components=4, split_sign=True, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("n feature names:", len(dl.get_feature_names_out()))
print("n transform columns:", dl.transform(X).shape[1])
print("float32 input -> output dtype:", dl.transform(X.astype(np.float32)).dtype)

pipe = make_pipeline(
    DictionaryLearning(n_components=4, split_sign=True, random_state=0), Ridge()
)
pipe.fit(X, y)
pipe.predict(X)
```


### Expected Results

```
n feature names: 8
n transform columns: 8
float32 input -> output dtype: float32
```
`pipe.predict(X)` returns an array of 60 predictions instead of raising.

The name count must match the transform width, the dtype should be preserved and a fitted pipeline should be able to predict.


### Actual Results

```
n feature names: 4
n transform columns: 8
float32 input -> output dtype: float64

```

```shell
        version: 0.3.34.0.0
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: Haswell

       user_api: blas
   internal_api: openblas
    num_threads: 12
         prefix: libscipy_openblas
       filepath: /home/sepurisaikrishna/sk-venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so
        version: 0.3.31.dev
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: Haswell

       user_api: openmp

    num_threads: 12
         prefix: libgomp
       filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0

```

### Interest in fixing the bug

yes

so while going through the file i found `sklearn/decomposition/_dict_learning.py:1149-1160`,
`_BaseSparseCoding._inverse_transform`, already accounts for `split_sign`:
```python
expected_n_components = dictionary.shape[0]
if self.split_sign:
    expected_n_components += expected_n_components
```
It expects `2 * n_components` and undoes the split. But `_n_features_out` in the same
file returns the unsplit count in all three classes:
- `SparseCoder` line 1412
- `DictionaryLearning` line 1750
- `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning` line 2334

**root cause**
1. those three `_n_features_out` properties
2. `_BaseSparseCoding._transform` allocates the split array as
   `np.empty((n_samples, 2 * n_features))`, no `dtype=`, so always float64
3. `DictionaryLearning.fit_transform` returns the raw code `V` and never applies the
   split (the other two classes have no `fit_transform` override, so they are fine here)

The reason its not caught yet is that `split_sign=True` has exactly one test in the suite,
`test_dict_learning_split` in `sklearn/decomposition/tests/test_dict_learning.py`, and it
only exercises `transform` and `inverse_transform` and no common test sets `split_sign=True`.

fix can be, make `_n_features_out` account for `split_sign` in all three,
allocate the split array with the input dtype, and have `fit_transform` apply the same
split `transform` does.

title: Impact of active wait policy of OMP implementations in scikit-learn
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

## About active wait in OpenMP

To my knowledge, there are two possible OpenMP implementations in scikit-learn:
- GNU OpenMP (libgomp): libgomp is the default one (i.e. the one packaged in PyPI build,
  and the one fetched by default in conda-forge). Its active wait behavior is controlled
  by `GOMP_SPINCOUNT` (an integer).
- LLVM OpenMP (libomp), for which active wait behavior is controlled by `KMP_BLOCKTIME` (a time in ms or us).
  It has a sibling: libiomp5 from Intel. They seem to resemble a lot as libomp is a fork of libiomp.

`GOMP_SPINCOUNT` and `KMP_BLOCKTIME` have the same role: control how long threads remain
actively waiting/spinning after the end of a parallel region.

These environment variables can dramatically hurt or help performance depending on the workload: if threads are still actively waiting when the next parallel region starts, entering it is much cheaper. Conversely, active waiting can pollute other threads/backends (e.g. OpenBLAS pthreads).

Inconveniently, libgomp reads `GOMP_SPINCOUNT` only once at initialization time unlike OMP_NUM_THREADS, which can be adjusted at runtime per workload.
libomp on the other hand, provides `kmp_set_blocktime` that seems to work like `omp_set_num_threads` (=> could
probably be used in a local context manager).

Also, in their recent versions, both libraries share a common policy for heterogeneous cores*: when such cores are detected, they set `GOMP_SPINCOUNT=1`/`KMP_BLOCKTIME=0`.
It was not the case a couple of years ago (at least for libgomp), which is why the libgomp bundled inside the scikit-learn PyPI wheel has `GOMP_SPINCOUNT=300000` (the default), see issue #34437 about why the PyPI wheel bundles an old-ish libgomp.
Otherwise the default values are:
- `GOMP_SPINCOUNT=300000`
- `KMP_BLOCKTIME=200ms`

Ok, so now that I said all that, what are the affected workloads in scikit-learn?
To my knowledge, there are mainly two: k-means and HGB.

### Impact on Kmeans

See the dedicated issue: #17334

But in short:

In Kmeans fit, we alternate OMP regions with BLAS regions.
So if:
- BLAS is OpenBLAS pthreads (true for PyPi wheel)
- OpenMP is libgomp, the active wait is enabled (`GOMP_SPINCOUNT=300000`)
- (repeated) small fits
Then you'll observe a dramatic slowdown (compared to other setups), the smaller the datasets
the worse it'll get. The example from the issue is 10-20x slowdown.

Note that the active wait of libomp is implemented differently and doesn't pollute
the openBLAS pthreads (even with `KMP_BLOCKTIME=200ms`).

### Impact on HGB

In HGB, we have many small OMP regions (around 10k for a typical fit, independently of the dataset size).

Hence, the overhead of handling threads can easily dominate, in that case active wait helps a lot
as it reduces this overhead.

Note that it doesn't solve the problem entirely (`prange`s still have an overhead,
even if threads are already awake and actively waiting), HGB still scales counter-productively
for small datasets, or deep trees, or large number of threads, ... But the `GOMP_SPINCOUNT=1`/`KMP_BLOCKTIME=0`
effect is dramatic, in my benchmarks it makes HGB fit 5-10x slower on a wide variety of standard small to medium-big datasets. This slowdown is observed by laptop users installing scikit-learn from conda-forge.

Scaling of HGB has its own dedicated issue:
- #14306: old but full of interesting and relevant ideas
- #30662: more recent and probably the observation of the `GOMP_SPINCOUNT=1`/`KMP_BLOCKTIME=0` effect mentionned just above.

----

*heterogeneous cores / hybrid CPUs are basically the norm for modern laptops nowadays.

title: BUG sample-weight ignored by `min_sample_leaf` in HGBDT
body:
## Description

In the following [course](https://probabl-ai.github.io/calibration-cost-sensitive-learning/content/notebooks/prevalence_correction.html#solution), we are using the weight of HGBDT to correct probability estimate. We know that it should be equivalent with a post-hoc correction. However, they are not equivalent for HGBDT while it works for logistic regression. In the past, we thought that it was due to the binning but it has been fixed (cf. #29641).

## Potential cause (to be check further)

`Splitter` in `sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/splitting.pyx` applies `min_samples_leaf` to histogram **counts** (`n_samples_left` / `n_samples_right`), not to the sum of sample weights (or hessians). Loss gradients/hessians (and bin edges after #29641) are weighted correctly.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1000,
    n_features=10,
    n_informative=5,
    n_redundant=0,
    weights=[0.75, 0.25],
    random_state=0,
)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
sw = rng.randint(1, 4, size=len(y))
X_rep, y_rep = np.repeat(X, sw, axis=0), np.repeat(y, sw)


def max_raw_diff(min_samples_leaf):
    est = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        min_samples_leaf=min_samples_leaf,
        early_stopping=False,
        max_iter=50,
        random_state=0,
    )
    weighted = clone(est).fit(X, y, sample_weight=sw)
    repeated = clone(est).fit(X_rep, y_rep)
    return np.max(np.abs(weighted._raw_predict(X) - repeated._raw_predict(X)))


print(max_raw_diff(1))   # ~1e-8
print(max_raw_diff(20))  # ~2.4, unexpected
```

Observed on `main` (`1.10.dev0`):

- `min_samples_leaf=1`: max `|raw_pred|` diff ≈ `4.6e-08`
- `min_samples_leaf=20`: max `|raw_pred|` diff ≈ `2.42`

## Expected behavior

Expect equivalence.

## Notes

- Documented limitation in `test_sample_weight_effect` (forces `min_samples_leaf=1`).
- Related: #26128 (histogram counts vs weights). Not a regression of #29641; remaining gap after that fix.

Attaching two ProgressBar instances on the same estimator breaks on teardown when the second one tries to `_run_queues.pop(context.root_uuid)`. 

I see two options to address the issue:

- Adding an attribute (maybe named `_unique`) to indicate that a callback can only have one instance attached to an estimator, and raising a `ValueError` if multiple are given to `set_callbacks`. This would also help the management of default callbacks in #34272 to ignore a default callback if one of the same unique callback was manually attached.

- Constraining all callback classes to work when multiple instances are attached to the same estimator and fix `ProgressBar` to do so. 

I have a preference for the first option, but I'd love to hear others' opinions.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The recent pytest update (9.1.1) introduces a warning in our scikit-learn compatibility tests for our own encoders. Our encoder inherits from scikit-learn’s `TransformerMixin` and `BaseEstimator`, and we use `sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.parametrize_with_checks` to verify that the custom encoders are compatible with scikit-learn.

The warning originates from `parametrize_with_checks`, which essentially returns a `pytest.mark.parametrize`. It currently passes a generator to `pytest.mark.parametrize`. However, this is deprecated in current versions of pytest.

It would therefore be useful to review or update the `parametrize_with_checks` implementation so that it no longer relies on the deprecated generator behavior. This will allow us in the future to keep testing for scikit-learn compatibility.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Run the following file using pytest's latest version (9.1.1):

```python
import pytest
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import parametrize_with_checks


@parametrize_with_checks([DummyRegressor()])
def test(estimator, check):
    check(estimator)
```

This can be run from terminal with `pytest name_of_file.py`


### Expected Results

The expected result is no warning about deprecation from pytest.
